claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The starting microstructure is hierarchical and organized into lamellar colonies with internal boundaries.
Dislocations pile up at internal boundaries during tensile loading.
Dislocation pile-ups produce local stress concentrations, brittleness, and premature failure.
A single-step controlled post-deformation anneal can modify the internal lamellar-colony boundaries.
An optimized annealing temperature and duration can promote partial recovery at lamellar interfaces without excessive coarsening or recrystallization.
Annealing will improve boundary coherence and spacing.
Improved boundary coherence and spacing will reduce dislocation accumulation at lamellar interfaces.
Recovery at lamellar boundaries will relieve local residual stresses.
Reduced dislocation pile-ups and local stresses will delay microcrack nucleation.
Avoiding coarsening will preserve solid-solution and boundary strengthening.
The annealed alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase its yield and tensile strengths relative to the untreated alloy.
Annealing parameters must be tightly controlled because annealing conditions can alter the microstructural length scale and phase constitution.
The proposed benefit applies to room-temperature tensile testing at standard strain rates.
The optimal annealing temperature and duration and the magnitude of the resulting property changes are presently uncertain.

contradictions.description: The treatment is called a post-deformation anneal, which presupposes a deformation step, but the experiment compares an as-cast set directly with an annealed set and specifies no prior deformation for the annealed samples.
